report.headline: Usage projected to fall from 19.3% to 15.7% in the NBA, with the efficiency projection carrying no signal at all

projection.text: The model projects a 15.7% usage rate in the NBA, down from 19.3% in the source G League season, against a target-league average of 20.1% (sd 5.2%), placing the point estimate nearly a full standard deviation below the typical NBA rotation player.

risks.text: Turnover rate was high at 23.4% in the source season, a concern that predates any league adjustment.
Even at the point estimate, projected usage of 15.7% sits roughly 0.85 standard deviations below the NBA average of 20.1% (sd 5.2%), implying a materially reduced offensive role.
The estimate rests on only 45 historical GL->NBA transitions, a thin base for a projection with this much spread.
The true shooting projection is built on a model that performs worse than simply assuming league-average efficiency, so no efficiency conclusion should be drawn from it.

strengths.text: Playmaking stood out in the source season, with a 25.8% assist rate and 6.21 assists per 75 possessions.
Scoring efficiency was well above the G League average, a 57.5% true shooting mark that sat +0.39 standard deviations above league norm.
The player belonged to a group that was already above-average by G League standards at the time of the move, sitting +0.27 sd above their league.

uncertainty.text: The 80% interval for usage runs from 10.4% to 20.9%, spanning more than two standard deviations of the NBA usage distribution, so the model can say this player projects below average but cannot pin down where; for true shooting the model's own error (4.7%) is no better than simply guessing the league mean, so the 53.0% true-shooting projection should not be treated as informative.
